1.title: Fundamentals of Energy Infrastructure
1.intro: The vocabulary chapter, and the one that quietly supplies the arguments for everything that follows. It starts with energy and its units, then builds the two economic ideas the whole lecture rests on: economies of scale and economies of scope. From there it defines infrastructure — material, institutional, immaterial — and its technical, economic and institutional characteristics. Networks bring compatibility and the network effect; prices bring the distinction between price, tariff, fee and charge. And because a grid is a natural monopoly, the chapter ends where it has to end: unbundling and regulation.
1.thread: Energy and units → economies of scale and scope → what infrastructure is → who invests in it → networks and compatibility → prices and pricing → natural monopoly and sub-additive costs → unbundling → regulation, its authorities and its five procedures → German and European energy law

2.title: Natural Gas as a Product
2.intro: Before you can transport, store or price gas, you have to know what it actually is. This chapter treats natural gas as a product: where it sits in the value chain, how it differs from electricity, what it is made of, and the parameters that decide whether two gases are interchangeable at all — gross and net calorific value, standard and norm conditions, the Wobbe index, H-gas versus L-gas. It closes with demand: gas consumption is temperature-driven, and that single fact is what makes storage necessary.
2.thread: Value chain and the comparison with electricity → composition and gas types → calorific values, standard conditions and the Wobbe index → quality parameters across Europe → uses and the temperature-correlated consumption profile

3.title: Natural Gas Transport
3.intro: The largest chapter of the gas block, and the one the exam draws on most. It has three movements. First the technology: pipeline components, capacity, and the economic trade-off between a larger diameter and more compressor stations. Then the alternative: the LNG chain, its cost split and the distance at which it beats a pipeline. Finally the commercial layer: how transport costs decompose into fixed and variable, what a transportation contract stipulates, and the three pricing systems — distance-related, entry-exit and postage stamp — with the calculations that go with them.
3.thread: Pipeline components and capacity → diameter versus compression → pressure along the line → the LNG value chain and its cost split → LNG versus pipeline over distance → fixed and variable transport costs → transportation contracts and the shipper's and transporter's tasks → pancaking → distance-related, entry-exit and postage stamp pricing

4.title: Natural Gas Storage
4.intro: Storage exists because demand swings and supply does not. This chapter starts with the parameters — cushion gas, working gas volume, injection and withdrawal rate — and the way they constrain each other, then names the three functions of storage: compensating demand fluctuations, compensating supply fluctuations, and economic optimisation. After the technology (depleted fields, aquifers, salt caverns) come security of supply, the contracts, the pricing formula and the flexibility components. It ends in the market: hub prices, location and time swaps, and the summer/winter spread that decides whether a storage booking pays.
4.thread: Storage parameters and their interdependence → the three functions → storage types and surface facilities → security of supply and the filling obligations → contracts and the pricing formula → flexibility: annual, seasonal and hourly components → EU, German and Austrian storage law → hub prices, location swap, time swap and the summer/winter spread

5.title: Oil and Oil Products
5.intro: The short block, kept deliberately compact by the lecture itself, but it is examined. Oil differs from gas in one decisive respect: it is not bound to a network, so four transport modes compete for the same cargo. The chapter covers the product and its value chain, the price history and refinery margins, then the comparison of pipeline, ship, rail and truck by capacity, cost, flexibility and safety. It closes with shipping contracts, freight rates and the German strategic stockholding obligation.
5.thread: Crude oil as a product, the value chain and price history → refinery margins and utilisation → the four transport modes compared → ships, freight rates and VLCC pricing → key elements of a crude oil shipping contract → oil storage and Erdölbevorratung

6.title: Introduction to Energy Systems Analysis
6.intro: The power block opens by asking what a model is for. The overall aim is stated once and holds for the rest: provide structured support for decisions in energy systems, politically and entrepreneurially. Then come the six steps of systems analysis, and the two great axes along which every energy model can be placed — bottom-up versus top-down, and optimisation versus simulation. Learn those two axes properly; almost everything later in the block is one quadrant of them.
6.thread: Why analyse energy systems at all → current challenges, macro and micro → what a model is and the six steps of systems analysis → bottom-up versus top-down → optimisation versus simulation → which questions each combination can answer

7.title: Optimal Unit Commitment
7.intro: Short-term planning: which plants run in which hour, and what does that make the price? The chapter builds it from the bottom — a linear programme with a graphical solution, then the electricity markets and their temporal classification, then the variable generation cost of a plant assembled from fuel, logistics, CO2 and auxiliary costs. Out of that comes the merit order and the single sentence that carries the exam: the marginal plant in each hour sets the price. The exercise at the end applies it to three plants under minimum-load and ramp constraints.
7.thread: A linear optimisation problem and its graphical solution → electricity markets in space and time → variable generation costs, item by item → individual versus system marginal costs → the merit order principle → cost-minimal load coverage with three plants, with and without technical constraints

8.title: Convolution
8.intro: The shortest chapter and one of the most reliably examined. Real power plants fail and need maintenance, so a deterministic dispatch overstates what the park can deliver. Convolution is the method that folds availability into the load duration curve: first the curve is transformed into steps of constant load, then each plant is convolved in, so that the residual demand curve seen by the next plant already reflects the outage probability of the ones before it. Know the two steps and be able to draw them.
8.thread: Why availability matters → transforming the load duration curve into steps → convolving in plant by plant → reading the graphical solution → what the result says about expected generation and unserved energy

9.title: Capacity Expansion Planning
9.intro: Long-term planning: not which plant runs, but which plant gets built. The green-field version is peak-load pricing — with annualised fixed costs and variable costs per technology you can derive the optimal capacity mix and the resulting average price. The chapter then supplies the inputs a real model needs: the existing plant park, expected technological development, and the two ways of quantifying progress — growth curves and experience curves with their learning rate. It ends on the modelling choice of perfect foresight versus a time-step approach.
9.thread: Why expand at all → peak-load pricing on a green field → the expansion exercise: annualised fixed costs, variable costs, optimal capacities, average price → plant park data and technology assumptions → growth curves → experience curves and the learning rate → perfect foresight versus time-step

10.title: Scenario Planning
10.intro: Long-horizon decisions cannot be optimised away, because the inputs themselves are unknown. Scenario planning is the lecture's answer: not a forecast, but a set of internally consistent futures that make the critical uncertainties visible. The chapter distinguishes top-down and bottom-up scenario construction, gives the six steps of a scenario process, and — this is the part that gets examined — shows the combination with energy systems analysis: uncertain parameters are bundled into a few aggregated drivers, and the scenarios are built on those.
10.thread: Uncertainty in long-term decisions → what scenarios do and do not do → top-down versus bottom-up scenario construction → the six steps → combining scenarios with energy systems analysis → aggregated drivers → short-, medium- and long-term effects on plant profitability

11.title: Investment Appraisal
11.intro: Four dynamic methods, one common root: money has a time value, so every cash flow has to be discounted before it can be compared. The chapter derives compounding and discounting, then works through net present value, the annuity method with its capital recovery factor, the internal rate of return and the discounted payback period — each on the same wind-farm example, which makes them easy to compare. The closing slides say what all four share and where they stop: they need assumptions, and they cannot price uncertainty.
11.thread: Time value of money, compounding and discounting → net present value → annuity and the capital recovery factor → internal rate of return and its graphical solution → discounted payback period → what the methods have in common and where their limits are

12.title: Decision Making under Uncertainty
12.intro: When probabilities are unknown, expected values are unavailable — so what do you decide on? The chapter separates the three decision environments (certainty, risk, uncertainty) and then applies five rules to the same payoff table: maximax for the optimist, maximin for the conservative, minimax regret via an opportunity-loss table, Laplace for equal likelihood, and Hurwicz as a weighted compromise. Practise applying them by hand — the exam asks you to compute, not to recite. The closing warning matters too: a rule can disguise the uncertainty it was meant to expose.
12.thread: Certainty, risk and uncertainty → the payoff table → maximax → maximin → minimax regret and the regret table → Laplace → Hurwicz and the coefficient of realism → what the rules hide, and why no automatism

13.title: Electricity Grids
13.intro: The physical half of the power block. It starts with alternating voltage, active and reactive power and the loss formula that explains the entire voltage hierarchy — losses fall with the square of the voltage, which is why long distances run at 380 kV. From there: the structure of the supply system and its voltage levels, the European interconnected grid and market coupling, the control-reserve ladder that keeps frequency at 50 Hz, storage options for electricity, and finally what makes an infrastructure “smart”.
13.thread: AC fundamentals, power and transmission losses → voltage levels and the hierarchy of the supply system → the European grid, UCTE tasks and market coupling → system services and the four control reserve levels → storing electricity → curtailment and smart grids

14.title: Hydrogen
14.intro: The third block opens with the question the whole hydrogen debate turns on: why do we need molecules at all when we could electrify directly? The answer is the set of applications that cannot be electrified — and the clean hydrogen ladder ranks them. The chapter then covers production by electrolysis with its three technologies and their efficiencies, the colour scheme, transport by re-used pipeline and by ship, and underground storage. The recurring theme is the gap between announced projects and installed capacity: about 2 GW of electrolysis against about 5,000 GW required by 2050.
14.thread: Why synthetic energy carriers → global demand today and in 2050 → the clean hydrogen ladder → electrolysis: alkaline, PEM, SOEC and their efficiencies → technology readiness → hydrogen colours, green versus blue → transport by pipeline and ship → underground storage → current projects, and the gap between announcement and reality

15.title: Hydrogen Derivatives
15.intro: Pure hydrogen is awkward to ship and store, so it gets converted. Each derivative in this chapter is one answer to that problem, with its own trade-off: ammonia buys transportability at the cost of toxicity and a conversion loss; methanol and Fischer-Tropsch fuels buy full compatibility with the oil infrastructure at the cost of needing a carbon source; LOHCs buy ambient-condition handling at the cost of carrier mass; synthetic methane inherits the whole natural gas world but loses the most energy on the way. Learn the reaction equations and the advantage/challenge pairs.
15.thread: Ammonia: conventional versus renewable production, Haber-Bosch, advantages and challenges → methanol: synthesis and the carbon capture it needs → LOHCs → synthetic methane and the re-use of the gas infrastructure → power-to-liquid and Fischer-Tropsch → for each: what it inherits, what it costs

16.title: Comparison, Shipping and Metal Fuels
16.intro: The chapter that ties the third block together, and the one whose comparison table is asked about directly. All the carriers are set side by side on energy density, safety, storage, ship transport and pipeline compatibility — and the pattern that emerges is simple: the more a molecule behaves like a fuel we already ship, the more infrastructure it inherits. After that come the efficiency and cost comparison of maritime supply chains, the decarbonisation of the shipping sector itself, and iron as an unexpected but serious energy carrier.
16.thread: Gravimetric and volumetric energy densities → the comparison table of all derivatives → efficiency and cost of maritime supply chains → adapting existing maritime infrastructure → shipping sector decarbonisation → metals as energy carriers and infrastructure re-use

units.intro: The starting vocabulary. Energy, work and power get separated, the units are put on one scale (J, Wh, toe, Btu and the decimal prefixes) and volumetric units are introduced — which matters more than it looks, because every gas calculation later starts by converting m³ into kWh. Take the unit conversions seriously here; half the calculation marks in the exam depend on them.

Two ideas that look similar and are not. Economies of scale: producing more of the same good lowers the average cost, because fixed costs spread and because a larger pipe carries disproportionately more gas. Economies of scope: producing two goods together costs less than producing each alone. Scale is the reason a grid is a natural monopoly; scope is the reason utilities bundle electricity, gas and services.

Jochimsen's three types — material, institutional, immaterial — plus the definition of critical infrastructure in Germany, and then the three sets of characteristics: technical, economic and institutional. The economic ones are the ones to memorise: high capital requirement, external effects, economies of scale, step costs and a high fixed-cost share. Both the type list and the economic characteristics have been examined directly.

Who builds and owns this stuff, and with whose money. Investors, funds and companies on one side; the actual investment volumes in the electricity grid, the gas distribution grids and hydropower on the other. Treat the figures as orders of magnitude rather than exam facts — what matters is the shape: infrastructure is capital-intensive, long-lived and increasingly financed by parties who never operate it.

The abstract layer under every later chapter. Transport and storage are defined as functions, then a network is defined as a graph of nodes and edges, and compatibility at the nodes turns out to be its precondition — physical, communication, and by convention. Add the network laws and the levels at which a network can be described. The compatibility triple has been an exam question in its own right.

Terminology that the exam likes because it is easy to get wrong. Price, tariff, fee, charge and contribution are not synonyms: they differ in who sets them, on what basis, and whether payment buys a service or a right. Pricing then gets its own slide — the mechanisms by which a price is arrived at, which is what the transport and storage chapters build on later.

The theoretical heart of the regulation half. A cost function is sub-additive if one producer can serve the combined output more cheaply than several — that is the formal definition of a natural monopoly, and it makes the network a monopolistic bottleneck. The answer is to separate the bottleneck from the competitive stages: unbundling, in its accounting, informational, functional, legal and ownership degrees. Know why the separation is needed, not just what it is called.

The most heavily examined section of chapter 1. Regulation creates “as-if competition” for the bottleneck; the trilemma of energy policy states what it is trying to balance; the Bundesnetzagentur and its European counterparts do the work. Then the five procedures: rate-of-return and cost-plus on the cost-based side, price cap, revenue cap and yardstick competition on the incentive-based side — each with its own characteristic failure mode, the Averch-Johnson effect being the famous one.

How the framework got here. The development of German energy law from the 1935 Energiewirtschaftsgesetz through liberalisation to the current regime, plus what the EU directives added. The price slides at the end give the payoff: what households and industry actually pay for electricity and gas, and how much of that is network charges, levies and tax rather than the commodity.

units.section: Natural gas: value chain and properties
units.intro: Natural gas as a product. The value chain from exploration to the burner tip, the comparison with electricity — storable, chemically bound, transportable in two states — and the family of gases that count as natural gas, including biomethane and SNG. This sets up the distinction that runs through the whole gas block: the molecule, the transport service and the storage service are three separate products with three separate prices.

The section with the most examinable definitions in chapter 2. Gross versus net calorific value, standard versus norm conditions, and the Wobbe index as the measure of interchangeability — two gases with the same Wobbe index deliver the same heat through the same burner at the same pressure. H-gas versus L-gas, the DVGW ranges and the European quality maps show why cross-border gas trade needs specifications at all.

Where the gas goes and, more importantly, when. Household and heating demand is temperature-correlated and therefore strongly seasonal; industrial profiles are flatter; some customers buy a flat band. This single asymmetry — production and pipelines want a constant load, consumption is anything but — is the reason the next two chapters exist.

The hardware and the vocabulary. Which components make up a pipeline system, the definitions a transport contract uses (entry point, exit point, third-party access), and how transport capacity is defined and measured. Note the orders of magnitude: up to 6,000 km, up to 1,400 mm diameter, up to 100 bar, compressor stations every 80 to 500 km.

The core trade-off of pipeline design, and a favourite of the examiner. The same capacity can be bought with more steel or with more compression, so the optimum is an economic compromise between diameter and the number of compressor stations. The pressure-versus-distance sawtooth is the picture to be able to draw; the influence of temperature and the energy cost of compression are the qualifications on top.

How a transport actually works contractually — gas is not tracked molecule by molecule, it is entered at one point and withdrawn at another — plus the terminology that goes with it. The historical maps of the European pipeline system, from 1970 to today, are context rather than exam material, but they explain why the entry-exit model had to replace point-to-point contracts.

One of the highest-yield sections in the gas block: the five stages from exploration through liquefaction, shipping and regasification to the customer, together with the cost split — 11 % production, 42 % liquefaction, 20 % transport, 27 % storage and regasification. Being able to draw the chain and name the most expensive step has been asked directly. Add the tank designs (Moss spherical, membrane) and the purchase strategies.

Where LNG actually flows, and the comparison that matters: LNG versus pipeline over distance. The ENI chart is the one to understand — LNG's cost curve is almost flat, a pipeline's rises with distance, so beyond a break-even distance LNG wins. The series of trade-flow maps for successive years is best learnt as one trend, not as six separate facts; the terminal maps for Europe and Germany are worth a glance for the post-2022 build-out.

The utilisation figures behind the capacity. Liquefaction and regasification plants are enormously capital-intensive, so load factors decide the specific cost — and European regasification terminals have historically run well below capacity. Read this as the empirical footnote to the LNG cost split: the 42 % and 27 % shares assume utilisation that is not always there.

How a transport tariff comes about. Costs split into fixed (pipes, planning, rights of way, compressors, metering, personnel, insurance) and variable (mainly compression energy), and the consequence is a high fixed-cost share, so specific cost falls sharply with utilisation. The two curves to understand: specific cost as a function of distance and capacity, and as a function of diameter and number of compressors.

The commercial mechanics. What a transportation agreement stipulates, how firm and interruptible capacity differ, and the division of labour between transporter and shipper — including the shipper's duty to nominate within its booked capacity and the balancing regime that catches deviations. Exceeding capacity and balancing are the two clauses that cost money in practice.

The section with the calculations. Three systems: distance-related (price × distance × capacity), entry-exit (entry price × entry capacity + exit price × exit capacity, with no route in the tariff at all) and postage stamp (one flat tariff for the whole network). Entry-exit is the European model and the one that removes pancaking — the cascading of tariffs across successive networks. Work the examples until the unit conversions are automatic.

The section that carries chapter 4. Total capacity splits into cushion gas and working gas volume; injection and withdrawal rates are the flows, and they depend on the filling level, so the three parameters cannot be chosen independently. Then the three functions: compensating demand fluctuations, compensating supply fluctuations, and economic optimisation. Both the parameter interdependence and the three functions have been exam questions.

Where the gas physically sits. Depleted fields and aquifers give large working gas volumes at low rates — seasonal storage. Salt caverns give small volumes at high rates and several cycles a year — peak shaving and trading. Above-ground storage is a different animal again. The surface facilities schematic explains what the compressors, driers and separators are for.

The political function of storage, and the one that changed most after 2022. Which tools exist, who is responsible for what, and how national storage capacity compares with national consumption across Europe. The capacity-tariff example in this section is the same one used in the official example exercise — treat it as an exam task, not as an illustration.

How a storage product is bought. Three components are booked and billed separately — injection rate, withdrawal rate and working gas capacity — and the total is their sum: T = p_inj·κ_inj + p_wd·κ_wd + p_wg·v_wg. Note the units: rates are capacity prices in €/kW/a, working gas is an energy price in €/kWh/a. The ambiguity-of-storage-prices slides show why two offers with different headline prices can be worth the same.

The most abstract section of the gas block, and pure diagram work. A storage product is bounded in three dimensions — an annual component, a seasonal component with a minimum and a maximum, and an hourly component with the same — and together they span the “area of flexibility” the customer has actually bought. Read the figures rather than the text here; the formulas only make sense against the shapes.

The legal layer that 2022 created. EU storage regulation with its filling targets, the German storage law and the Austrian variant with its strategic storage management and tendered products. The point to take away: storage moved from being a purely commercial asset to a regulated instrument of security of supply, with obligations attached.

Where storage meets the market. A hub product has a price and a delivery period; a location swap moves gas in space without transporting it, a time swap moves it in time without storing it. The storage principle (p_supply + p_storage < p_sales) and the swap condition (p_supply − p1 < p_sales − p2) are the two inequalities to know. The summer/winter spread decides whether any of it pays.

units.section: Crude oil: product, value chain and prices
units.intro: Oil as a product: density and sulphur content define the grade, the value chain runs from reserves through refining to products, and the price history — 1861 to today — shows a volatility no gas market matches. Refinery margins and utilisation explain why product prices and crude prices move apart. Learn the structure; the individual price points are context.

The comparison the exam asks for. Four modes — pipeline, ship or barge, rail, truck — ranked by magnitude (up to 1.5 million bbl/day for a pipeline, up to 750 bbl for a truck), by specific cost, by flexibility and by safety. Because oil is not bound to a network, the modes genuinely compete, which is exactly what makes the comparison examinable.

The commercial side of moving oil by sea. Ship classes and cargo dimensions, how freight rates are quoted and how volatile they are, and the key elements of a crude oil shipping contract — laytime, demurrage, transfer of title and risk. The VLCC price series shows how much of the delivered price can be freight when the market tightens.

Short but concrete. Commercial oil storage on one side, and on the other the German Erdölbevorratung — the statutory 90-day stockholding obligation and the agency that runs it. The parallel to gas storage regulation is deliberate: both are cases where the state overrides the commercial optimum in the name of security of supply.

units.section: Motivation and goals of energy systems analysis
units.intro: Why model at all. The macro challenges (renewables expansion, regional imbalance, voltage stability, security of supply) and the micro perspective set the scene, then the overall aim is stated in a form worth memorising: provide structured support to guide decision processes in energy systems, politically and entrepreneurially. The learning-objective slides in this section are the lecturer telling you what will be asked.

What a model is — a target-oriented, simplified representation of reality — and the six steps of systems analysis, from formulating the problem and drawing the system boundary through model development, validation and application. Electricity is an unusually convenient object for this because it is homogeneous and its production processes are well defined.

units.section: Model types: bottom-up, top-down, optimisation, simulation
units.intro: The two classification axes of the entire block. Bottom-up energy process models resolve technologies and are strong on technical detail; top-down energy economic models resolve the economy and are strong on feedback effects. Independently of that, optimisation models search for the best decision under constraints, while simulation models reproduce behaviour. Be able to place any named model in that grid, and to say what it can and cannot answer.

A two-product production problem solved graphically: objective function, constraints, feasible region, and the optimum at a vertex. It exists to make the standard form (max c'x subject to Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0) concrete before it gets applied to power plants. If the graphical solution is clear here, the dispatch exercise later is bookkeeping.

units.section: Energy markets and the electricity value chain
units.intro: The market landscape. The value chain from generation to retail, the spatial classification of markets, and — the part that gets examined — the temporal classification of German power markets: futures, day-ahead, intraday, balancing. The household price breakdown at the end shows how little of the retail price the wholesale market actually sets.

The centre of gravity of the whole power block. Variable generation cost is built up item by item — fuel and logistics divided by efficiency, plus CO2 cost divided by efficiency, plus auxiliary costs — and the worked hard-coal example gives 50.35 €/MWh_el. Then the distinction between an individual generator's marginal cost and system marginal cost, and the merit order principle: everyone bids variable cost, the marginal plant sets the price. Fuel and CO2 prices determine the order, which is why a CO2 price can trigger a fuel switch.

The exercise the exam reuses. Three plants (30, 40 and 60 €/MWh_el, computed from the data in the first part), a twelve-hour load, and the task of covering it at minimum cost — first unconstrained, then with minimum stable levels, then with ramp limits. Watch what happens to total system expenses and to marginal costs as each constraint is added: they rise, and the marginal-cost pattern stops following the merit order.

Two steps, one method. Step 1 transforms the load duration curve into a shape with steps of constant load. Step 2 convolves the plants in one by one, so that each subsequent plant sees a residual curve that already accounts for the outage probability of the ones ahead of it. The result is an expected generation per plant and an expected unserved energy. Be able to draw both steps and to say why a deterministic dispatch overstates what the park delivers.

The framing question: enough capacity available, or new capacity needed? Short-term dispatch takes the plant park as given; expansion planning treats it as the decision variable. The learning objectives stated here define what the rest of the chapter has to deliver — including being able to explain perfect foresight versus time-step approaches.

units.section: Peak-load pricing on a green field
units.intro: The clean theoretical case. On a green field, with annualised fixed costs and variable costs known per technology, you can derive which technology should cover which slice of the load duration curve: high fixed and low variable costs for base load, the reverse for peak. The screening-curve logic behind it is what makes the exercise in the next section solvable.

Four parts, each worth practising by hand: annualised fixed costs per technology, variable generation costs, the installed capacities of an ideal supply system, and the resulting average power price. The last part is the one students skip and the exam likes — the average price in an optimal system is not the marginal cost of the peak plant.

units.section: Power plant park and technological development
units.intro: What a real expansion model has to be fed. The existing European park aggregated into technology classes, the historical generation mix for calibration, expected fuel and CO2 price paths, and estimates of how technologies will develop — with batteries flagged as the potential game changer. The point: model outputs are only as good as this exogenous input layer.

How technical progress gets quantified. Growth curves describe diffusion over time; experience curves describe cost as a function of cumulative production, with a constant percentage cost reduction per doubling — the learning rate. On log-log axes that is a straight line, which is why the PV example is shown twice, linear and logarithmic. Know the mechanisms behind the effect (learning by doing, scale, technical improvement) and the honest caveat the lecture adds: the approach still lacks a theoretical foundation.

A short section that is asked about directly. Perfect foresight knows all input assumptions over the whole horizon and optimises everything simultaneously — the true optimum, but unrealistic. The time-step approach knows only the current step and inherits what earlier steps built — realistic, path-dependent, and generally not optimal. Be ready to give two characteristics and one advantage and one disadvantage of each.

Why the method has to change with the horizon. Utilities plan online, under a year, one to five years and beyond five years, and uncertainty grows along that axis while the appropriate method shifts from deterministic optimisation through stochastic approaches to scenario planning. The “selected planning tasks of utilities” figure that summarises this has been an exam question in its own right — learn it well enough to label it blank.

What scenarios are for: acknowledging uncertainty and exposing the critical, ambiguous drivers — explicitly not producing a single most likely answer. Top-down builds a consistent story, bottom-up combines parameter values; the six-step construction process sits on top. The governmental and the entrepreneurial perspective want different things from the same set, which is why the number of scenarios is itself a design decision.

units.section: Combining scenario planning and energy systems analysis
units.intro: The synthesis the chapter exists for. Energy systems analysis supplies the quantitative model, scenario planning supplies the input futures, and together they answer questions no single run can — for instance the ceteris paribus effect of a CO2 price increase on the profitability of a pumped storage plant.

units.section: Scenario construction for power plant investments
units.intro: The method made concrete. Many uncertain parameters (fuel prices, CO2 price and policy, renewables expansion, demand) are bundled into a few aggregated drivers, scenarios are spanned on those drivers, and the effect on plant attractiveness is read off — separately for short and medium term and for the long-term green-field view. The pumped-storage example shows the mechanism: a flatter merit order means lower price volatility means a worse case for storage.

The foundation for everything else in the chapter. A euro today is not a euro in ten years: compounding carries a value forward by (1+i)^t, discounting brings it back by dividing. The savings-account illustration is trivial on purpose — the point is that every subsequent method is this one operation applied to a cash-flow series.

Discount every cash flow to t = 0 and sum. NPV > 0 means the investment earns more than the required rate of return, so it is worth doing; between alternatives, the higher NPV wins. The wind-farm example runs through the whole calculation, and the practical note matters: in practice the discount rate used is a required rate of return, not a market interest rate.

The same information, expressed as an average yearly amount. Built on the net present value and turned into a uniform annual series by the capital recovery factor — the table for which is given on the slide. Use it when alternatives have different lifetimes, because comparing annual equivalents is fairer than comparing totals.

The interest rate at which the net present value becomes zero. There is no closed-form solution for a general cash-flow series, so it is found numerically or graphically — the lecture shows both. Read the IRR as a break-even return: the project pays as long as the required rate stays below it.

How long until the discounted cash flows have repaid the investment. It answers a risk question rather than a profitability one, which is why it is used alongside NPV and never instead of it — it says nothing about what happens after the payback point.

The closing synthesis: what all four methods share (assumptions about cash flows, lifetime and discount rate), where they differ, and where they collectively stop. They cannot price uncertainty, and they cannot handle non-monetary criteria — which is exactly the hand-off to the scenario chapter and to decision rules under uncertainty.

Three types, and the whole chapter depends on telling them apart. Under certainty the outcome is known; under risk the states of nature have probabilities, so expected values work; under uncertainty they do not, so you need a decision rule instead. Get the classification right and the rules that follow are mechanical.

Five rules on one payoff table. Maximax picks the best of the best (optimist); maximin the best of the worst (conservative); minimax regret needs an opportunity-loss table built first and then minimises the largest regret; Laplace treats all states as equally likely and takes the average; Hurwicz weighs best and worst with a coefficient of realism. Practise computing all five on the same table — and remember the closing warning: applying a rule can disguise the uncertainty it was supposed to reveal.

The physics that explains the grid's architecture. Single-phase alternating voltage, active and reactive power, resistance and the loss calculation the lecture works with: I = P/U and P_loss = I²·R, which collapses to P_loss = R·P²/U². Losses fall with the square of the voltage — that single relation is the reason for the extra-high-voltage level, and it has been an exam calculation.

units.section: Structure of the power grid and voltage levels
units.intro: The hierarchy from generation through transmission and distribution to the customer, with the four voltage levels and what each is for. Grid losses of roughly 4.7 % including transformation put a number on the previous section, and the network expansion cost estimates from the NEP show what the transition costs in concrete.

Why the European grids are synchronised, what the UCTE structure was set up to achieve — better frequency maintenance, mutual support in emergencies, smaller reserve holdings — and how day-ahead and intraday market coupling allocates cross-border capacity. Physical interconnection and market integration are two different things; the section keeps them distinct.

Two slides, high exam yield. Electricity cannot be stored in bulk, so feed-in and withdrawal must match permanently and any imbalance shows up as a frequency deviation from 50 Hz. The control reserve ladder — primary, secondary, tertiary and hourly reserve — is graded by activation time, with the TSO responsible up to one hour and the balancing group beyond. Note the labelling error on the figure: the second band reads “Primary control” but is secondary control.

What can actually store electrical energy, at which power, for how long and at what annuitised cost per kW. Pumped hydro is the reference; the merit-order illustration shows how a storage plant earns its money by pumping in the cheap hours and turbining in the expensive ones — which is exactly the spread argument from the gas storage chapter, in another market.

units.section: Smart grids and the future power supply
units.intro: Why “smart” at all: wind curtailment is the concrete symptom, and the development curve shows it growing. The closing slides list the smart elements of a future supply system — measurement, communication, controllable loads and decentral generation — as the answer to a grid that was designed for one-directional flow and now carries the opposite.

The framing of the whole third block. Direct electrification wins wherever it is possible, so synthetic carriers exist for what is left: fertiliser, refining, steel, shipping, aviation, high-temperature heat. The clean hydrogen ladder ranks those applications, and the demand projections — about 110 Mt/a today, several hundred by 2050 — come with an explicit warning about how far the sources diverge.

Where the hydrogen economy actually stands. Today's production is almost entirely grey and almost entirely a chemical feedstock; hydrogen is barely traded across borders because it is expensive to move. The European market slide sets up the transport and infrastructure sections that follow.

The production section, with the numbers the exercises use. Alkaline at about 4.7 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 64 % against the lower heating value), SOEC at about 3.6 kWh/Nm³ (≈ 83 %), PEM in between, each with its own maturity and flexibility. The reality check on the same slide: about 2 GW installed worldwide by the end of 2024, against roughly 5,000 GW needed by 2050.

The colour scheme — green, blue, grey, turquoise and the rest — as a shorthand for feedstock and emissions, plus the technology readiness levels and the green-versus-blue comparison. Geological (white) hydrogen appears as the wildcard. Know what each colour means in terms of process and CO2, not just the palette.

Two routes, both compromised. By pipeline: re-using natural gas transmission lines costs 10–35 % of new construction, but hydrogen embrittles steel and blending limits are real. By sea: liquefaction at −253 °C, constant boil-off, and exactly one prototype carrier in existence. The European Hydrogen Backbone is the concrete plan built on the first route.

Salt caverns are the proven option — tight, chemically inert, high cycling rate — while porous formations raise questions about microbial activity and gas losses that gas storage never had to answer. Compare the volumes involved with the gas storage figures from chapter 4: the same infrastructure logic, a much less convenient molecule.

The project landscape, and a deliberate reality check — the lecture titles part of it “Hope or Hype?”. Phase targets for European electrolysis, the hydrogen strategies of fossil-fuel exporting countries, R&D activity and the backbone investment. The transferable content is the phase figures and the gap between announced and installed capacity, not the individual company slides.

The honest list: low volumetric energy density, high liquefaction energy (about 2.9 kWh/kg for compression alone, far more for liquefaction), flammability and safety, no existing infrastructure, and roughly 9 kg of water per kg of hydrogen — 18 including cooling. The exercise slides at the end are worth doing by hand; the official solution sheet is the model for how the exam expects a calculation to be laid out.

The best-developed derivative, and the one with the fullest exam coverage. Conventional production in three steps — steam reforming, water-gas shift, Haber-Bosch — versus the renewable route of electrolysis, air separation and Haber-Bosch. Know the equations, the conditions (400–450 °C, 120–220 bar, iron catalyst, under 20 % conversion per pass) and the stoichiometry (1 kg NH3 needs 0.18 kg H2). Then the trade-off: excellent transportability and an existing terminal network, against toxicity, corrosiveness and NOx.

The derivative that inherits the oil world. Liquid at ambient conditions, so ordinary tanks and tankers work, and it is already the highest-volume chemical commodity shipped worldwide. The catch is carbon: methanol synthesis needs a CO2 source, via the reverse water-gas shift and then CO + 2 H2 → CH3OH, which makes carbon capture — point source or direct air — part of the process rather than an add-on.

Hydrogen chemically bound to a liquid carrier that stays liquid at ambient conditions, is hardly flammable and can travel in existing oil infrastructure. The price is paid in mass and heat: the carrier is transported both ways, and dehydrogenation needs high-temperature energy at the destination. Compare directly against pure hydrogen — the lecture puts them side by side for a reason.

The derivative with the best infrastructure story and the worst efficiency. SNG re-uses the complete natural gas world — pipelines, roughly 260 TWh of storage, power plants, heating systems, ships — but every additional conversion step costs energy, and methane is itself a strong greenhouse gas if it leaks. The LNG infrastructure slides here connect the third block back to chapter 3.

The route to drop-in liquid fuels. Syngas — hydrogen and carbon monoxide in roughly a 2:1 ratio, made via the endothermic reverse water-gas shift — is converted in the Fischer-Tropsch process into hydrocarbons that need no infrastructure adaptation at all, which is what makes them the candidate for aviation. The cost development curve is the sobering part.

The section built around one table, and that table has been examined directly. Hydrogen, ammonia, methanol, LOHCs, methane and Fischer-Tropsch fuels compared on safety, storage, ship transport and pipeline compatibility, plus the economic and efficiency comparison of the maritime supply chains. The pattern to state in one sentence: the more a molecule behaves like a fuel we already ship, the more infrastructure it inherits.

Shipping is both the transport mode for these fuels and a customer for them. The global fleet, its emissions, and the vessels already running on methanol, hydrogen or ammonia — the count of which is the point: a handful, mostly first-of-a-kind. Read this section as the demand side of everything in chapter 15.

The genuinely surprising ending. Iron powder as a storable, non-toxic, high volumetric energy density carrier that burns to iron oxide and can be reduced back with hydrogen — closing a loop that needs no carbon at all, re-uses coal power plant sites and ships as ordinary bulk cargo. Compare its supply cost against the other carriers before dismissing it.
